method: Re-run of the census at the repaired gate. Every rule was judged by the real gate binary, standing in its own project, with the SAME probe the first census used — the probe is stored beside the rule so the measurement can be repeated. Each probe was driven through TWO binaries back to back in the same pass: the commit the published census was measured at (b384d6a) and HEAD, so the difference is the code and not the clock. A rule that did not answer in its own name got a second pass, alone in a scratch guard, to separate a dead rule from one a neighbour catches first. Nothing was executed: every probe is a PreToolUse event on stdin, asserted with a canary file the gate was asked to delete and did not. The generator is site/rule_census.py.

by_mechanism.note: The rule is capable — it refuses this command when it stands alone in a guard of its own — but an earlier rule in the same guard catches the same command first, so this id can never appear in a refusal.

mechanisms_tested_and_not_found.claim: every bash deny regex containing > is dead because the parser carries redirections separately from argv
mechanisms_tested_and_not_found.result: NOT REPRODUCED at this commit. The structural laws in baseline.h read words only, but a deny REGEX reads Seg.surface, which still carries > >> and tee. 17 of the 18 bash rules on this machine whose pattern contains a redirection fire; the 18th is shadowed, not dead.

mechanisms_tested_and_not_found.claim: gate.cpp reads the guard from the exact session cwd with no walk up, so from a subdirectory none of a project's rules load
mechanisms_tested_and_not_found.result: REPAIRED at this commit. Re-measured with the same fixture shape, built inside a checked-out worktree so it sits under a `.git` (a fixture in the system temp area measures the deliberate absence of a bound, not the reach of the guard): at the project root old=reach-no-yarn new=reach-no-yarn; one directory down old=None new=reach-no-yarn; two down old=None new=reach-no-yarn. It never appeared in the per-rule census either way, because it switches every rule in a guard off at once rather than one rule.
mechanisms_tested_and_not_found.exposure_note: Of the Bash/tool events on this machine that ran inside a guarded project, 10.0% ran from a subdirectory where that project's own rules did not load (11,091 of 111,074). The home baseline guard is worse by construction: its root is $HOME, so it loads only when the cwd is exactly ~ — 61.4% of home-scoped work (47,278 of 76,980) ran with its 7 rules absent.

protection_actually_lost.note: A dead rule id does not always mean a dead protection: some have a second rule in the same guard that catches the file anyway. The rest have nothing behind them.

incident_authored.note: A rule marked authoredBy: incident was written because something really happened. A dead one means that thing can happen again.

over_fires.note: The other direction: rules that refuse work they were never written about. An allow twin is the author writing down what the rule must NOT catch. Every twin on this machine was re-run against BOTH binaries, because the repairs widen what a rule is matched against and a rule that starts refusing honest work costs more than one that never fires. The 26 ordinary and 50 benign commands are carried forward from the first census and were not re-run here.
over_fires.allow_twins_withheld_note: A git-push twin at a pushGate guard is not a judgement: gate.cpp forks a shell and RUNS the project's suite before deciding, so driving it executes cargo test / go test / bin/rspec and moves lastTestVerified between the two binaries. Withheld from both runs so both binaries answer the same question.

tail -1/-2 clips the 'X% tests passed' verdict line, making green runs unreadable as pass/fail; use tail -5 or grep 'tests passed'. REPAIRED 2026-08-03: the old pattern was 'ctest[^|]*\|\s*tail\s+-(n\s*)?[12]\b' and could never fire — rabadon matches each rule against a PARSED SEGMENT surface and a '|' is the segment boundary, so no surface ever contains one (measured: gate exit 0 on 'ctest --test-dir engine/build | tail -1'). The tail segment is judged alone, so the ctest context is not visible; the pattern therefore fires on a bare 'tail -1' with no file operand, which is the piped shape. 'tail -1 Logs/run.log' and 'tail -20' still pass.

ctest -N / --show-only only LISTS tests and runs nothing; its exit code is 0 whatever the suite does, so it is never a pass/fail signal — run the real suite. REPAIRED 2026-08-03: the old pattern was 'ctest\s+-N\b.*grep\s+-c' and could never fire, because it needed the pipe and the parsed surface splits on it (measured: gate exit 0 on 'ctest -N | grep -c Test').
